new_statements.quote: Yala (Ikom) is a terraced-level language with three contrastive, tonal registers: high, mid, and low. Said another way, it is a terraced-level language with a mid tone which is independent of any down-step or latent tone. The tonetic pitches that occur on the various syllables of any tone-phrase are the result of the combined effect of three inter-acting systems: the register system, the downdrift system, and the terracing or downstep system. The overall system of tonal inter-action is organized with respect to the tone phrase, which may be one word, several words, or a whole sentence.
new_statements.citation: Armstrong, Robert G. 1968. Yala (Ikom): a terraced-level language with three tones. Journal of West African Languages 5(1): 49-58.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (10 pp., image-only scan) and its 300-dpi scanned. The quoted §3.0 passage is on p. 50 (PDF page 2) exactly as given; I rendered the page and read it visually — the only difference from the quote is the original's line-break hyphen in "terracing or down-step system", i.e. verbatim in substance. The paper (presented Lagos 1967; data from one speaker, Mr. Erim O. Erim) is a pure tone analysis: §3.0 three contrastive registers H/M/L organised over the tone phrase; §4.1 initial L raised before H/M; §4.2 H+L realised as H+falling with lengthening; §5 downdrift; §6 downstep/latent tone; §7 pitch interplay; §8 comparison with Igbo. Grep of the whole scanned (stress|accent|prominen|emphas|in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yala (Ikom) is described purely as a three-register tone language (H, M, L) with downdrift and downstep organised over the tone phrase; the source never mentions word stress, accent or prominence, so no stress placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: H+L sequence surfaces as falling tone with vowel lengthening (§4.2); utterance-initial L before H/M is realised low-mid (§4.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone phrase (one word, several words, or a whole sentence); word-level stress not addressed. Data from one speaker of Yala (Ikom).
new_statements.identity_note: Armstrong 1968 describes Yala (Ikom), the variety called Nkum near Ikom (c. 6,000 speakers in 1967), which he explicitly distinguishes from Yala (Ogoja) and Yala (Obubra); it is the only one of the three with downdrift and downstep. Glottolog 5.1/5.3 has a single languoid yala1263 with no separate dialect codes, so the statement applies to yala1263 but strictly to its Ikom dialect. Oko 1986 (University of Calabar) does not name its variety in the pages read; Bunkowske's work is on Ogoja Yala.
